rationale: A wins because it keeps the strongest story pinned to the only rare asset in the update: "Duolingo says beta users talked to its AI character for nine minutes at a stretch." B is good, but "Duolingo adds chess, testing whether its habit machine works beyond language" starts converting one course launch into a grand platform thesis before the proof exists. A is less cute and more defensible; that is usually what gets the email answered.
gaps_in_A: "first public engagement figure for it" is not supplied. The nine-minute figure is supplied; "first public" needs proof.
"free beginner chess course" adds "beginner" without support. The update only says a chess course launches free for all users.
"A large consumer learning app putting a free beginner chess course in front of its entire user base" is directionally fair, but the chess angle still needs course scope before a chess outlet cares.

"Duolingo's daily active users hit a record" is dismissed a little too fast; a record DAU claim from a profitable public company could support a short markets item if the absolute number and source document exist.
gaps_in_B: "AI cartoon" and "talking cartoon" are punchy, but the update says character Lily, not cartoon. Cute wording is not a fact substitute.
"habit machine works beyond language" and "learning anything" stretch one chess launch into a platform thesis. That may become the story, but the update does not prove it yet.
"priciest tier" and "flagship AI feature" are unsupported. The facts say paid Max subscribers get the feature, not that Max is the priciest tier or that this is Duolingo's flagship AI bet.
The first and third angles both lean on Max exclusivity plus AI-video monetization, so the distinction is weaker than advertised even though the target desks differ.
